items.basis: The proposed spacer-induced turbulence mechanism fails to address the primary fouling mechanism in municipal wastewater MBRs, which is not just shear stress but also concentration polarization and gel layer formation as evidenced by the long-term study in doi:10.1007/s11356-026-38139-3, which shows soluble microbial products form irreversible layers regardless of shear conditions.

The candidate completely fails to define critical boundary conditions including wastewater characteristics (variable COD, TSS, viscosity), temperature fluctuations, and required flux rates that would determine whether the spacers can maintain sufficient turbulence under all operational conditions as required for municipal systems.

The candidate's own evidence contradicts the proposal, as doi:10.30684/etj.30.19.14 demonstrates that standard hollow fiber MBRs already achieve acceptable performance for municipal wastewater without spacers, and doi:10.1016/j.desal.2009.09.140 shows that air sparging is more effective than passive spacers for fouling control.

The candidate provides no evidence that spacer modification would outperform the baseline, as evidenced by the absence of comparative data in the evidence bundle, making it impossible to determine if the intervention actually reduces fouling beyond the status quo.

The design cannot be implemented because hollow fiber membranes require precise packing density for optimal surface area-to-volume ratio, and adding spacers would necessarily reduce packing density, contradicting the fundamental engineering principle of maximizing membrane surface area in confined reactor volumes as implied by the compact design in doi:10.1016/j.memsci.2007.06.026.

The testable prediction focuses only on transmembrane pressure increase but fails to specify critical measurement parameters including flux rate, temperature, wastewater composition, and cleaning frequency, making it impossible to determine if any observed pressure changes are due to the spacers or confounding variables.
